PREFACE 
Î
have long had a passion for Greek myths, so when a letter came 
four years ago from Cassell, asking whether I would like to write 
their Dictionary of Classical Mythology, I had no hesitation in 
replying with a resounding 'Yes!'.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: INTRODUCTION For centuries people have spoken of the Greek myths as of something to be rediscovered, reawoken.
text_raw:
INTRODUCTION 
For centuries people have spoken of the Greek myths as of something 
to be rediscovered, reawoken.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The truth is, it is the myths that are still out there waiting to wake us and be seen by us, like a tree waiting to greet our newly opened eyes.
text_raw:
The truth is, it is the myths that 
are still out there waiting to wake us and be seen by us, like a tree 
waiting to greet our newly opened eyes.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Roberto Calasso, The Marriage of Cadmus and Harmony yths were at the heart of ancient Greek life and culture.
text_raw:
Roberto Calasso, The Marriage of Cadmus and Harmony 
yths were at the heart of ancient Greek life and culture.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: They held a central place in poetry at public and private festivals, and were told and retold by the poets, changing and developing as time went by, and from the sixth century BC onwards forming the subject of gripping dramas played out on the tragic stage.
text_raw:
They held a central place in poetry at public and private 
festivals, and were told and retold by the poets, changing 
and developing as time went by, and from the sixth century BC onwards 
forming the subject of gripping dramas played out on the tragic stage.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But these myths were more than mere stories.
text_raw: But these myths were more than mere stories.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: To the Greeks they were history, telling of real people in the real past; and a man's genealogy, often originating from a divine mythical ancestor, showed his place in the world and his relation to the great heroes of myth 1.
text_raw:
To the Greeks they were 
history, telling of real people in the real past; and a man's genealogy, 
often originating from a divine mythical ancestor, showed his place in 
the world and his relation to the great heroes of myth 1.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Myths too were portrayed in the visual arts: on wall paintings, now all lost, in sculptures, and above all on the pots that were an integral part of everyday life, since Greek vase-painters were (luckily for us) the most prolific illustrators of myth.
text_raw:
Myths too 
were portrayed in the visual arts: on wall paintings, now all lost, in 
sculptures, and above all on the pots that were an integral part of 
everyday life, since Greek vase-painters were (luckily for us) the most 
prolific illustrators of myth.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Even the physical world - rivers, springs, woods, mountains, the very earth itself - was alive with divine pres­ ences; and in the time of Homer, whose Iliad and Odyssey give us our first recorded myths, the gods still walk among men.
text_raw:
Even the physical world - rivers, springs, 
woods, mountains, the very earth itself - was alive with divine pres­
ences; and in the time of Homer, whose Iliad and Odyssey give us our 
first recorded myths, the gods still walk among men.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In due course, after the Roman conquest of Greece, the Romans adopted these Greek myths.
text_raw:
In due course, after the Roman conquest of Greece, the Romans 
adopted these Greek myths.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: They took over, for instance, the whole Olympian hierarchy of gods, together with their mythologies, and grafted them where possible on to their own Italian divinities.
text_raw:
They took over, for instance, the whole 
Olympian hierarchy of gods, together with their mythologies, and 
grafted them where possible on to their own Italian divinities.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: As Horace famously pronounced, "Greece, taken captive, captured her savage conqueror" (Epistles 2.1.156).
text_raw:
As 
Horace famously pronounced, "Greece, taken captive, captured her 
savage conqueror" (Epistles 2.1.156).

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Often the Romans made their own unforgettable adaptations of the Greek originals (Virgil's Dido comes at once to mind, or of some of the brilliant metamorphoses in Ovid), but on the whole they added few new myths of their own.
text_raw:
Often the Romans made their 
own unforgettable adaptations of the Greek originals (Virgil's Dido 
comes at once to mind, or of some of the brilliant metamorphoses in 
Ovid), but on the whole they added few new myths of their own.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: 10 Introduction Together this body of Greek and Roman myths forms the 'Classical Mythology' of our title.
text_raw:
10 Introduction 
Together this body of Greek and Roman myths forms the 'Classical 
Mythology' of our title.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: It covers the widest range of human experience.
text_raw: It covers the widest range of human experience.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Compare, for instance, the bloody violence of Atreus and his kin with the simple goodness of Philemon and Baucis, or the comic fate of Midas with the tragic fate of Pentheus, or the very different loves and lusts shown in the myths of Admetus and Alcestis, of Tereus, of Hero and Leander, of Myrrha, or of Ceyx and Alcyone.
text_raw:
Compare, for 
instance, the bloody violence of Atreus and his kin with the simple 
goodness of Philemon and Baucis, or the comic fate of Midas with 
the tragic fate of Pentheus, or the very different loves and lusts shown 
in the myths of Admetus and Alcestis, of Tereus, of Hero and Leander, 
of Myrrha, or of Ceyx and Alcyone.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Small wonder, then, that classi­ cal myths have lived on with a perennial vitality, becoming a con­ tinuing inspiration for creative artists through the ages.
text_raw:
Small wonder, then, that classi­
cal myths have lived on with a perennial vitality, becoming a con­
tinuing inspiration for creative artists through the ages.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Ancient authors explored complex issues of social and personal identity through the medium of myth, and ever since then these myths have stirred and shaped and enriched the Western imagination, becom­ ing inextricably woven into the fabric of our culture.
text_raw:
Ancient 
authors explored complex issues of social and personal identity 
through the medium of myth, and ever since then these myths have 
stirred and shaped and enriched the Western imagination, becom­
ing inextricably woven into the fabric of our culture.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Always they have provided a rich vein of of metaphor and imagery for artists of all kinds, down the centuries until the present day.
text_raw:
Always they 
have provided a rich vein of of metaphor and imagery for artists of all 
kinds, down the centuries until the present day.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Fluid and adaptable, they have been used time and again to give fresh insights into mankind's changing experience in a changing world.
text_raw:
Fluid and adaptable, 
they have been used time and again to give fresh insights into 
mankind's changing experience in a changing world.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In recent years there has been a tremendous resurgence of interest in this mythol­ ogy, so this book has been written both as a celebration of a vital and fascinating subject, and as a key to the world of classical myth for anyone wishing to delve more deeply into its many delights.
text_raw:
In recent years 
there has been a tremendous resurgence of interest in this mythol­
ogy, so this book has been written both as a celebration of a vital 
and fascinating subject, and as a key to the world of classical myth for 
anyone wishing to delve more deeply into its many delights.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: My aim has been to retell the myths as readably as possible, detail­ ing any major variants and including, where appropriate, my own translations from ancient writers to give life to my narrative.
text_raw:
My aim has been to retell the myths as readably as possible, detail­
ing any major variants and including, where appropriate, my own 
translations from ancient writers to give life to my narrative.

text: He later went on the CALYDONIAN BOARHUNT; here his fellow-Argonaut PELEUS accidentally killed Eurytion, then came to Iolcus to be purified of blood-guilt by his friend.

text: Unfortu­ nately Astydameia fell in love with Peleus and tried to seduce him, and when he rejected her advances she accused him to her husband of trying to rape her.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Acastus, unwilling to kill the man whom he had purified, took him hunting on Mount Pelion in the hope that there he would meet his death, and even stole his sword while he was asleep, leaving him alone and defenceless against the wild Cen­ taurs.
text_raw:
Acastus, unwilling to kill the man whom he 
had purified, took him hunting on Mount Pelion in the hope that 
there he would meet his death, and even stole his sword while he

taurs.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But Peleus was saved by the kindly Centaur Cheiron and so lived to take his revenge: he sacked Iolcus with the help of Jason and the DIOSCURI, then killed Astydameia and marched his army into the city between the severed halves of her corpse.

text_raw:

Acarnania and Aetolia, rising in central Epeirus and flowing into the

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Homer calls it the 'prince of rivers' (Iliad 21.194), and certainly it was the most important in cult and legend.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Like all river- gods, Achelous was the son of OCEANUS and Tethys, and he himself was the father of the SIRENS, of Calirrhoe, the second wife of ALCMAEON, and of the nymphs of two famous springs, Peirene at Corinth and Castalia at Delphi.
text_raw:
Like all river-
gods, Achelous was the son of OCEANUS and Tethys, and he himself 
was the father of the SIRENS, of Calirrhoe, the second wife of 
ALCMAEON, and of the nymphs of two famous springs, Peirene at 
Corinth and Castalia at Delphi.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At the mouth of the Achelous lie the Echinades Islands.
text_raw: At the mouth of the Achelous lie the Echinades Islands.

text: These had originally been five nymphs who forgot to honour the great river-god in their festivities.
text_raw:
These 
had originally been five nymphs who forgot to honour the great

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In his anger he swept them away and they were transformed into islands.
text_raw:
In his anger he swept them away and 
they were transformed into islands.

Another island, a little apart 
from the rest, was especially dear to Achelous, for this had once been

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: After she was seduced by the river-god, her indignant father flung her from a cliff into the sea, but Achelous caught her and held her up as she swam.

by the river-god, her indignant father flung her from a cliff into the

to his prayers she was changed into an island by Poseidon.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Achelous wished to marry DEIANEIRA, the daughter of Oeneus, king of Calydon, and he wooed her in three monstrous manifestations.
text_raw:
Achelous wished to marry DEIANEIRA, the daughter of Oeneus, king 
of Calydon, and he wooed her in three monstrous manifestations.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: 'He came in three shapes to ask my father for my hand', says Deianeira in Sophocles' Women ofTrachis (10-17), 'now manifest as a bull, now a shimmering, coiling snake, now with a man's body and a bull's head, and from his shaggy beard flowed streams of water from his springs.
text_raw:
'He came in three shapes to ask my father for my hand', says Deianeira 
in Sophocles' Women ofTrachis (10-17), 'now manifest as a bull, now 
a shimmering, coiling snake, now with a man's body and a bull's 
head, and from his shaggy beard flowed streams of water from his 
springs.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Expecting a suitor like that, I was always praying, poor crea­ ture, that I might die before ever I came near his bed.' But another suitor appeared, the mighty HERACLES, and wrestled with Achelous for Deianeira's hand.
text_raw:
Expecting a suitor like that, I was always praying, poor crea­
ture, that I might die before ever I came near his bed.' But another 
suitor appeared, the mighty HERACLES, and wrestled with Achelous 
for Deianeira's hand.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The river-god changed his shape unavailingly and Heracles vanquished him, breaking off as he did so one of the god's horns.
text_raw:
The river-god changed his shape unavailingly 
and Heracles vanquished him, breaking off as he did so one of the 
god's horns.

chapter_title: Frontmatter

To recover this, Achelous gave in its place the horn of

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: 50 Aeneas many allies flock to join him, including MEZENTIUS, an exiled Etruscan king, the virgin-warrior CAMILLA, leader of the Volscians, AVENTINUS, a son of Hercules, and CAECULUS, the founder of Praeneste.
text_raw:
50 Aeneas 
many allies flock to join him, including MEZENTIUS, an exiled Etruscan 
king, the virgin-warrior CAMILLA, leader of the Volscians, AVENTINUS, a 
son of Hercules, and CAECULUS, the founder of Praeneste.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Aeneas, anxious and disheartened, is encouraged in a dream by the god of the River Tiber.
text_raw:
Aeneas, anxious and disheartened, is encouraged in a dream by 
the god of the River Tiber.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In the morning he finds, just as the god promised, the white sow prophesied by Helenus lying on the river- bank with her thirty piglets, a sign that on this spot Ascanius will found a city thirty years later, and will call it Alba Longa ('Long White') after the sow.
text_raw:
In the morning he finds, just as the god 
promised, the white sow prophesied by Helenus lying on the river-
bank with her thirty piglets, a sign that on this spot Ascanius will 
found a city thirty years later, and will call it Alba Longa ('Long 
White') after the sow.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: On the god's instructions, Aeneas rows up the Tiber to Pallanteum, a city on a hill that will later be the Palatine Hill of Rome, and asks its king, the Arcadian EVANDER, to be his ally.
text_raw:
On the god's instructions, Aeneas rows up the 
Tiber to Pallanteum, a city on a hill that will later be the Palatine 
Hill of Rome, and asks its king, the Arcadian EVANDER, to be his ally.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Evander welcomes him, and although he himself is too old to fight, he entrusts his dear son PALLAS (4) to Aeneas and provides a large con­ tingent of cavalry for his war with the Latins.
text_raw:
Evander welcomes him, and although he himself is too old to fight, 
he entrusts his dear son PALLAS (4) to Aeneas and provides a large con­
tingent of cavalry for his war with the Latins.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Aeneas is also aided by the Etruscan king TARCHON, who becomes his ally out of hatred for the exiled Mezentius, and by Venus, who has new and splendid armour made for her son by Vulcan.
text_raw:
Aeneas is also aided 
by the Etruscan king TARCHON, who becomes his ally out of hatred 
for the exiled Mezentius, and by Venus, who has new and splendid 
armour made for her son by Vulcan.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: While Aeneas is away, Turnus and his army advance on the Trojan camp.
text_raw:
While Aeneas is away, Turnus and his army advance on the Trojan 
camp.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: They try to fire the ships, but these have been made from the pines of Mount Ida, haunt of the Phrygian goddess Cybele.
text_raw:
They try to fire the ships, but these have been made from the 
pines of Mount Ida, haunt of the Phrygian goddess Cybele.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She turns the ships into nymphs and they swim far away.
text_raw:
She turns 
the ships into nymphs and they swim far away.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The Rutulians besiege the camp, and during the night NISUS (2) and Euryalus try to get through their lines to summon Aeneas.
text_raw:
The Rutulians besiege 
the camp, and during the night NISUS (2) and Euryalus try to get 
through their lines to summon Aeneas.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: They slaughter many of the sleeping enemy, but are themselves killed, even as Nisus courageously tries to save his comrade.
text_raw:
They slaughter many of the 
sleeping enemy, but are themselves killed, even as Nisus courageously 
tries to save his comrade.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: When Aeneas returns with his reinforcements, Turnus attacks.
text_raw: When Aeneas returns with his reinforcements, Turnus attacks.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Pallas leads his men into the thick of the battle and is killed by Turnus himself, who now wears his belt as a battle spoil.
text_raw:
Pallas leads his men into the thick of the battle and is killed by Turnus 
himself, who now wears his belt as a battle spoil.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Aeneas, full of grief for his young ally, rages through the enemy ranks seeking revenge, but Juno has lured Turnus away from the battlefield to safety.
text_raw:
Aeneas, full of grief 
for his young ally, rages through the enemy ranks seeking revenge, but 
Juno has lured Turnus away from the battlefield to safety.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Aeneas wounds the Etruscan king Mezentius, then reluctantly kills his son Lausus, who tries to save his father.
text_raw:
Aeneas 
wounds the Etruscan king Mezentius, then reluctantly kills his son 
Lausus, who tries to save his father.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The grief-stricken Mezentius mounts his faithful horse, Rhaebus, for a last attack on Aeneas, but both horse and rider are killed.

mounts his faithful horse, Rhaebus, for a last attack on Aeneas, but

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The Aeneid ends with the death of Turnus, but we know that Aeneas now made peace with the Latins and married Lavinia, found­ ing the city of Lavinium in her name and ruling over a union of Latins and Trojans.

text_raw:

children, six sons who were married to six daughters, and they all 
lived happily together on their island paradise, completely free from

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: To this island came ODYSSEUS and his men, and for a month they were feasted royally by Aeolus and his family.

To this island came ODYSSEUS and his men, and for a month 
they were feasted royally by Aeolus and his family.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Then came the time to leave, and Aeolus was able to help Odysseus since he had been made guardian of the winds by Zeus.
text_raw:
Then came the 
time to leave, and Aeolus was able to help Odysseus since he had 
been made guardian of the winds by Zeus.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: He kept them in a cave on his island and could release them as he wished or as some god instructed, just as once before, on Hera's command, he had helped the ARGONAUTS with a gentle wind for their homeward voyage.

gave to Odysseus all the boisterous winds sewn up in a leather bag,

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Since Theseus was often said to be the son of POSEIDON, various explanations were given as to how this came about: either this was a story invented by Pittheus to save his daughter's credit; or Poseidon visited Aethra on the same night as Aegeus; or Aethra was inspired in a dream by Athena to cross to the neighbouring island of Sphaeria, where Poseidon came to her, and the name of the island was there­ after changed to Hiera, 'Holy Island', on which Aethra set up a temple to Athena Apaturia, 'the Deceitful'.
text_raw:
Since Theseus was often said to be the son of POSEIDON, various 
explanations were given as to how this came about: either this was a 
story invented by Pittheus to save his daughter's credit; or Poseidon 
visited Aethra on the same night as Aegeus; or Aethra was inspired 
in a dream by Athena to cross to the neighbouring island of Sphaeria,

text: But he was still maddened by the Furies, and the land of Psophis became barren because it harboured a matricide, so once more he consulted the Delphic Oracle.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Alcmene, a girl of exceptional beauty, was married to Amphit­ ryon, but she refused to consummate their marriage until he had avenged the deaths of her eight brothers, killed by the Taphians during a cattle raid.
text_raw:
Alcmene, a girl of exceptional beauty, was married to Amphit­
ryon, but she refused to consummate their marriage until he had 
avenged the deaths of her eight brothers, killed by the Taphians 
during a cattle raid.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Not surprisingly, her husband set off with alacrity on an expedition against the Taphians, and was on the point of arriv­ ing home, triumphant and laden with booty, when Zeus saw his moment.
text_raw:
Not surprisingly, her husband set off with alacrity 
on an expedition against the Taphians, and was on the point of arriv­
ing home, triumphant and laden with booty, when Zeus saw his 
moment.

text: He came to Alcmene at Thebes disguised as Amphitryon and recounted the victory over the Taphians.
text_raw:
He came to Alcmene at Thebes disguised as Amphitryon 
and recounted the victory over the Taphians.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Delighted to hear of it and completely taken in, she welcomed him to her bed.
text_raw:
Delighted to hear of it 
and completely taken in, she welcomed him to her bed.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Zeus even prolonged the night to three times its usual length, by persuading the Sun-god HELIOS not to rise for three days, so that he might enjoy Alcmene to the full.
text_raw:
Zeus even 
prolonged the night to three times its usual length, by persuading 
the Sun-god HELIOS not to rise for three days, so that he might enjoy 
Alcmene to the full.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: As soon as Zeus left, Amphitryon himself arrived and was amazed to find, when he went to his wife's bed, that she knew all about his victory and was sure that she had already slept with him.
text_raw:
As soon as Zeus left, Amphitryon himself arrived and was amazed 
to find, when he went to his wife's bed, that she knew all about his 
victory and was sure that she had already slept with him.

Bewildered,

done.

human flesh.

chapter_title: Frontmatter

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Atreus and his brother THYESTES, the eldest and most famous sons of PELOPS and Hippodameia, were destined to a tragic and bloody feud with one another, perhaps because of the curse of MYRTILUS on Pelops and his family, perhaps because of the curse of Pelops him­ self on his own children after their murder of CHRYSIPPUS.

Atreus and his brother THYESTES, the eldest and most famous 
sons of PELOPS and Hippodameia, were destined to a tragic and bloody 
feud with one another, perhaps because of the curse of MYRTILUS on 
Pelops and his family, perhaps because of the curse of Pelops him­
self on his own children after their murder of CHRYSIPPUS.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In Homer's Iliad alone there seems to be harmony between the brothers, in the peaceful transition of power from one to another by means of the ancient and hallowed royal sceptre (2.100-8).

text: In one version it was provided by HERMES, as a way of causing trouble in revenge for the death of his son Myrtilus, and it gave its possessor the right to the throne.
text_raw:

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Atreus had owned it and had become king, but when Aerope gave it to Thyestes, he was able to take the throne in his brother's place.

gave it to Thyestes, he was able to take the throne in his brother's

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In the second version, ARTEMIS caused the lamb to be born after Atreus had vowed to sacrifice to her the best of his flock, but when he saw the lamb he ignored his vow, and killed it, and put it in a chest.

text_raw:
Atreus, of course, agreed,

156 Atreus

chapter_title: Frontmatter

onciliation.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Many plays have been lost, all bar frag­ ments, but we know that Sophocles wrote an Atreus and a Thyestes in Sicyon, plus one (possibly two) Thyestes plays, and that Euripides wrote a Cretan Women and a Thyestes.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: As for extant tragedies, these often contain substantial references to the myth, as, for instance, Euripides' Electra 699-746, where the chorus sing of Aerope betraying Atreus by giving Thyestes the golden lamb, and of Zeus reversing the course of the sun and the stars in support of Atreus.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But perhaps the most memorable dramatisation that we possess is Aeschylus' Oresteia trilogy, where Thyestes' curse on the house of Atreus forms a bloody and violent background to the bloody and violent events enacted on and off stage - the murder of Agamemnon by Clytemnestra with the support of Aegisthus, the murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus by Orestes, and the pursuit of Orestes by the Furies, raging at the murder of his mother.

most memorable dramatisation

ITHS, another Thessalian tribe, men who were as civilised as the Cen­

text: Hostilities began when Ixion's son PEIRITHOUS became king of the Lapiths on his father's death, and the Centaurs claimed a share in the rule because Ixion was their grandfather.

first dispute, however, was settled peaceably, and when Peirithous

chapter_title: Frontmatter

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The legend was a favourite with poets from Homer onwards and was given a variety of treatments, but it is in fifth-century tragedy that it comes fully into its own, with the Clytemnestra of Aeschy­ lus' Oresteia trilogy (Agamemnon, Libation Bearers, Eumenides, 458 BC) dominating the extant literature that deals with the story.
text_raw:
The legend was a favourite with poets from Homer onwards and 
was given a variety of treatments, but it is in fifth-century tragedy 
that it comes fully into its own, with the Clytemnestra of Aeschy­
lus' Oresteia trilogy (Agamemnon, Libation Bearers, Eumenides, 458 BC) 
dominating the extant literature that deals with the story.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Prior to Aeschylus, Aegisthus and Clytemnestra were, as far as we can tell, joint partners-in-crime in Agamemnon's murder, with Aegisthus taking the dominant role; but in the Agamemnon, Aegisthus' part in the murder has dwindled into relative insignificance and he has become a blustering weakling who appears onstage only at the end of the play.

the murder has dwindled into relative insignificance and he has

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In Sophocles she is depicted as a truly evil woman: she rejoices in the murder of her husband; she is cruel to Electra; she would earlier have killed Orestes if Electra had not saved him; and in the play she gloats when she believes him dead, since she may now suppose herself safe for ever from retribu­ tion.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Demeter, one of the twelve great Olympian gods, was the Greek goddess of corn and thus the great sustainer of life for men and beasts alike.
text_raw:
Demeter, one of the twelve great Olympian gods, was the 
Greek goddess of corn and thus the great sustainer of life for men 
and beasts alike.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She was identified by the Romans with Ceres.
text_raw: She was identified by the Romans with Ceres.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: One of the six children of the Titans CRONUS and Rhea, she was swallowed and later regurgitated by her cannibalistic father.
text_raw:
One 
of the six children of the Titans CRONUS and Rhea, she was swallowed 
and later regurgitated by her cannibalistic father.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: To her brother ZEUS she bore a daughter, PERSEPHONE, also known as Kore ('the Girl'), with whom she was closely associated in Greek cult, the two of them often being called simply 'the Two Goddesses', or even 'the Demeters'.
text_raw:
To her brother ZEUS 
she bore a daughter, PERSEPHONE, also known as Kore ('the Girl'), with 
whom she was closely associated in Greek cult, the two of them often 
being called simply 'the Two Goddesses', or even 'the Demeters'.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Mother and daughter frequently appear together in ancient art, often holding torches and wearing crowns, sometimes holding sceptres and stalks of grain.
text_raw:
Mother and daughter frequently appear together in ancient art, often 
holding torches and wearing crowns, sometimes holding sceptres 
and stalks of grain.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The principal myth of Demeter concerns Persephone's abduction by HADES (i), the god of the Underworld, and her own long search for her beloved daughter.
text_raw:
The principal myth of Demeter concerns Persephone's abduction 
by HADES (i), the god of the Underworld, and her own long search 
for her beloved daughter.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The story is first told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.
text_raw:
The story is first told in the Homeric Hymn 
to Demeter.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Hades' desire to have Persephone for his wife was sup­ ported by Zeus, but because Demeter would have been violently against the match, he could not openly woo his chosen bride.
text_raw:
Hades' desire to have Persephone for his wife was sup­
ported by Zeus, but because Demeter would have been violently 
against the match, he could not openly woo his chosen bride.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Instead he snatched her up one day as she was gathering flowers, speeding with his chariot out of a chasm in the earth and carrying her down into his realm below.
text_raw:

he snatched her up one day as she was gathering flowers, speeding 
with his chariot out of a chasm in the earth and carrying her down 
into his realm below.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: While she could still see the light of the sun, Persephone cried out for her mother, and Demeter, hearing her, sped towards the sound as swift as a bird.
text_raw:
While she could still see the light of the sun, 
Persephone cried out for her mother, and Demeter, hearing her, sped 
towards the sound as swift as a bird.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But she was too late, for Perse­ phone had disappeared.
text_raw:
But she was too late, for Perse­
phone had disappeared.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: For nine days and nights Demeter wandered the earth with flaming torches in her hand, seeking her daughter.
text_raw:
For nine days and nights Demeter wandered 
the earth with flaming torches in her hand, seeking her daughter.

text: On the tenth day she met the goddess HECATE, who had also heard Persephone's cries, and together they went to the Sun-god HELIOS,

text: He told them of the abduction, adding that it had Zeus' approval and reassuring Demeter that Hades was a worthy husband for her daughter; but Demeter was so angry that she deserted OLYMPUS and the dwellings of the gods, and went to live among mor­ tals disguised as an old woman.

He told them of the abduction, adding that it 
had Zeus' approval and reassuring Demeter that Hades was a worthy 
husband for her daughter; but Demeter was so angry that she deserted 
OLYMPUS and the dwellings of the gods, and went to live among mor­

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In her wanderings she came to Eleusis in Attica, where the wife of King Celeus, METANEIRA, took her into her home as nurse to her baby son, Demophon.
text_raw:

King Celeus, METANEIRA, took her into her home as nurse to her baby 
son, Demophon.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The goddess' spirits were cheered by the jokes of the old serving woman, IAMBE, and she laughed for the first time since the loss of her daughter.
text_raw:
The goddess' spirits were cheered by the jokes of 
the old serving woman, IAMBE, and she laughed for the first time since 
the loss of her daughter.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: In gratitude for the kindness shown her, Demeter began to make her infant charge immortal, secretly burn­ ing away his mortal part in the fire each night, and anointing him with ambrosia each day.
text_raw:
In gratitude for the kindness shown her, 
Demeter began to make her infant charge immortal, secretly burn­
ing away his mortal part in the fire each night, and anointing him 
with ambrosia each day.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: But one night Metaneira interrupted her and cried out, horrified at seeing her little son in the fire.
text_raw:
But one night Metaneira interrupted her and 
cried out, horrified at seeing her little son in the fire.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At once Demeter rebuked her soundly and reassumed her divine splendour.
text_raw:
At once Demeter 
rebuked her soundly and reassumed her divine splendour.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Telling Metaneira what the Eleusinians must do to regain her favour, she left the house.
text_raw:
Telling 
Metaneira what the Eleusinians must do to regain her favour, she left 
the house.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Celeus and his people built the goddess a great temple, and here she lived for a whole year, still shunning Olympus.
text_raw:
Celeus and his people built the goddess a great temple, 
and here she lived for a whole year, still shunning Olympus.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Now in her grief she made the whole earth barren.
text_raw:
Now in 
her grief she made the whole earth barren.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: No corn would grow and a great famine afflicted mankind, so that Zeus feared there would soon be no men left to sacrifice to the gods.
text_raw:
No corn would grow and 
a great famine afflicted mankind, so that Zeus feared there would 
soon be no men left to sacrifice to the gods.

text: He sent mis as his mes­ senger to Demeter, ordering her to Olympus, but she refused to come.

text: He sent all the gods, one by one, to offer her gifts and plead with her, but still she refused.
text_raw:

but still she refused.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: At last he saw that he would have to bring Perse­ phone back from Hades, so HERMES fetched her up to the light of day.

text: But before she left, Hades secretly gave her pomegranate seeds to eat.
text_raw: But before she left, Hades secretly gave her pomegranate seeds to eat.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Mother and daughter were reunited with great joy; but because Persephone had eaten while in the Underworld, she could not leave it completely and was obliged to spend four months of every year with Hades.
text_raw:
Mother and daughter were reunited with great joy; but because 
Persephone had eaten while in the Underworld, she could not leave 
it completely and was obliged to spend four months of every year 
with Hades.

text: These were the months when winter gripped the land and the seed lay dormant within the earth.
text_raw:
These were the months when winter gripped the land 
and the seed lay dormant within the earth.

text_raw:

spring and summer months of life and growth and harvest, Perse­
phone lived joyously with her mother.

text: Demeter, accepting this com­ promise, now made the earth bring forth rich harvests once again.
text_raw:
Demeter, accepting this com­

text: She returned to Eleusis, and provided the Eleusinian TRIPTOLEMUS with a supply of corn and a chariot drawn by winged dragons.

with a supply of corn and a chariot drawn by winged dragons.

text: During her long search for her daughter, an Athenian called PHYTALUS gave her hospitality and she rewarded him with the gift of the first fig tree.

her long search for her daughter, an Athenian called PHYTALUS gave 
her hospitality and she rewarded him with the gift of the first fig

text: She also stopped at a cottage to ask an old woman for a drink and was given some barley water.
text_raw:

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She gulped it down so thirstily that the woman's cheeky son, ASCALABUS, taunted her with being greedy.
text_raw:
She gulped it down so thirstily that 
the woman's cheeky son, ASCALABUS, taunted her with being greedy.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She threw the dregs of the drink over him and turned him into a lizard.

She threw the dregs of the drink over him and turned him into a

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She also turned ASCALAPHUS (i), who disclosed the fact that Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds while in the Underworld, into an owl.

pomegranate seeds while in the Underworld, into an owl.

text: When Tan­ talus served his son PELOPS in a stew to the gods, testing their omnis­ cience, they all knew what had happened and refused to eat, except for Demeter.

When Tan­

In her grief for Persephone she absentmindedly ate part

text: Not so happy was the sorry fate which the impious ERYSICHTHON suf­ fered.

Not so happy was the sorry fate which the impious ERYSICHTHON suf­
fered.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Demeter punished him for cutting down trees in her sacred grove by afflicting him with such a raging, insatiable hunger that he eventually died by gnawing away at his own flesh.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: She lay with IASION (i), the son of Zeus and Electra, in a thrice-ploughed field in Crete, and bore him a son, PLUTUS, 'Wealth', who symbolised the wealth and good fortune, both vegetable and mineral, that springs from the earth.
text_raw:

wealth and good fortune, both vegetable and mineral, that springs 
from the earth.

text: It was sometimes said that she bore Iasion a second son, Philomelus, who invented the plough to prepare the earth for grain.

text: Although the details of the rites were successfully kept secret, it seems that they centred around Demeter's search for her lost daughter, and Persephone's return and reunion with her mother, symbolising both the rebirth of the crops in spring, and the mystic rebirth of the ini­ tiates after death.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
